description: Open source personal agent with its own computer. It chases invoices, preps your calls and cancels trials on real websites, and asks before it acts. Runs on your machine with the model you choose. By n8n.

files.content:
# Docs media

The Trust and Vault tour and six screenshots use the current app components with synthetic API data: four of Usage, one of Vault and one of a private form. The capture has no backend, model connection or connected account. Fields for private values stay empty. The tour states that the model check can make mistakes.

From the repository root, with dependencies installed:

```sh
pnpm run build
node docs/media/capture.mjs
node docs/media/compose.mjs
```

Capture needs Google Chrome. Set `NOD_MEDIA_CHROME` if its path differs from the macOS default. The command writes temporary files to `.local/nod-media`. It refuses a page error, an unknown API request or an old product name.

Composition needs macOS `say` with the Daniel voice, plus `ffmpeg`. It records each sentence with one voice, adds matching captions, and joins complete scenes with a short fade. It does not paint labels over an earlier video.

To select another output folder, pass it as the first argument to both commands. The second argument to `compose.mjs` selects the video asset folder. After visual review, copy the six PNG files from the output `screens` folder to `docs/src/assets/screens`.

The other screenshots and banners retain their original synthetic content. Their text edits use the app font and move the following text to keep normal word spacing.

Verify the result with OCR, then review each screenshot, every video scene, each transition, captions and browser playback. Run `pnpm --dir docs build` to check the site and its links. Fixture checks do not prove live sign-in or payment completion.

# Video links

To download or save a video from a link (X, TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, Facebook, LinkedIn, Bluesky and most other sites), run `save-video URL` in bash right away, without manage_apps list, the browser or sign-in checks. It saves an H.264/AAC MP4 that plays everywhere and fits the 50 MB limit for sending it in chat apps, and prints one JSON line per file. Call share_file for each file, then reply in one short sentence that names the video; mention a note, such as compression, only when the output has one. Pass yt-dlp options after the URL when needed, such as `--download-sections "*1:00-2:30"` for part of a long video or `--playlist-items 2` for one video of a post. For audio only, run `yt-dlp -x --audio-format mp3 -o "%(title).60B.%(ext)s" URL` and share the file. When the video is for work in the workspace, such as a transcript or a cut, run `save-video --full URL`: it keeps the full length and quality and is not for sharing.

If it fails, give the reason in one sentence. Private, deleted, age-restricted, region-blocked or DRM-protected videos cannot be saved, and a post without a video has nothing to save. For a long video or a recorded broadcast, offer to save a section, or use `--full` when the video stays in the workspace; a live stream can be saved after it ends. If the site is unsupported, open the page in the browser, read the video's direct media URL and run save-video on it once. Do not repeat a failed command.

--- title: MCP servers, APIs and CLIs description: Connect Notion, Linear and n8n through their MCP servers, and let Nod set up other services through an MCP server, an HTTP API or a command-line tool. sidebar: order: 4 --- Besides [Composio apps](/connect/apps/), Nod connects to Notion, Linear and n8n through their own MCP servers. For other services, it can set up an MCP server, an HTTP API or a command-line tool (CLI). These built-in MCP apps use the same folder format as community apps. Browse their [app pages](/connect/community-apps/), or follow [Creating your own connectors](/contribute/apps/) to add one. ## Notion and Linear Notion and Linear connect through their own hosted MCP servers, the same way as any [other MCP server](#connect-another-service). Open **Apps**, select **Connect** and sign in. If the service ends sign-in with an error, Nod shows that error, with secrets removed. If an older **Notion MCP** account appears in **Apps** but cannot read pages, connect **Notion** again. After the new connection works, disconnect the old **Notion MCP** account. Its earlier sign-in does not transfer to the direct connection. If you ask Nod in chat, it sends a link to a private setup page in Nod, and you start the sign-in there. The service's sign-in link never appears in the chat, so the model and chat apps never see it. If sign-in is cancelled or fails, select **Try again** in the connection dialog. Select **Start again** if you closed the sign-in window. Finish in the newest window, then dismiss the confirmed connection with **Done**. Nod can use every tool these servers offer, so it can read and change pages, issues and projects. Each change goes through the same [trust check](/trust/approvals/) as any app action. If Nod can't refresh a sign-in because it expired or was revoked, **Apps** shows **Sign-in required** with **Reconnect** from then on. ## n8n Nod builds, tests and changes n8n workflows and n8n Agents through your n8n instance's MCP server. Open **Apps**, select **Connect** on n8n and enter your n8n address, such as `https://you.app.n8n.cloud` or `localhost:5678`. Nod opens n8n's own sign-in and consent page. To use an access token instead, open **Use an access token instead** and paste the token from n8n under **Settings**, **Instance-level MCP**. This is the instance-level MCP token. An n8n API key doesn't work here. If n8n answers at `http://localhost:5678` from Nod's server, the form opens with that address filled in. Nod checks only that address when the form opens, and connects only when you select **Connect n8n**. If n8n doesn't answer, turn on MCP access in n8n under **Settings**, **Instance-level MCP**, and try again. The address can be on Nod's computer or its local network, such as a self-hosted n8n. Inside Docker, `localhost` refers to Nod's container. Only an address you enter or confirm yourself can be local, never one the model proposes. Nod sends that connection's requests and its token only to that address. Browser sign-in can also use a sign-in service at another address when that address is public and uses HTTPS on the standard port. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` count as the same address when the port matches, because n8n can name itself either way. Nod loads n8n's tools only when a task needs them and follows n8n's own guide for its tools, plus a short [n8n task guide](/how-it-works/skills/). It writes workflow code to a file in its workspace, checks it with n8n, then creates and tests the workflow with sample data before it reports back. A test doesn't run the steps that send or write to another service, so Nod checks the data each of those steps would have sent. Each n8n action goes through the [trust check](/trust/approvals/), like every app action. See [Build with n8n](/use/n8n/) for what to ask. ## Connect another service Search **Apps** by service name. If it isn’t listed, select **Ask Nod** on the **Connect another tool** card for help setting it up. To connect an MCP server yourself, open **Apps** and select **Connect MCP**. Enter a name of up to 80 characters, such as `Work email (n8n)`, and the server URL, then choose browser sign-in, an access token or an API key. Select **Continue** to finish authentication in the private setup dialog. For any MCP server, including Notion, Linear and n8n, the dialog shows the service's reason if sign-in can't start. When the server ends sign-in with an error, the dialog shows that error, with secrets removed. Only a sign-in you decline counts as cancelled. **Connection details** shows any extra setup instructions. Tokens stay outside the chat. To rename a server you added with **Connect MCP**, open **Apps**, open **Manage accounts** on the server’s card, and select **Rename**. The new name applies to every account on that card. You can search for it in Apps or ask for it by name in chat. The URL can be a public HTTPS address or, when you type it yourself, an address on your own computer or network, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp` or a Tailscale name. Without `http://` or `https://`, Nod uses HTTPS. A public HTTPS address you type can also use a port other than 443. In the desktop app, `localhost` is your computer. Inside Docker, it is Nod's container. A private address stays bound to the origin you entered, also when you reconnect. HTTP is allowed only for private addresses. With browser sign-in, the server's sign-in service can be at another address only when that address is public and uses HTTPS on the standard port. Connections that Nod proposes in chat must use a public HTTPS address. Nod connects to MCP servers over Streamable HTTP. When a server refuses it with a client error other than 401 or 403, Nod tries the older HTTP+SSE transport at the same address, with the same checks. If that also fails, the error shows the Streamable HTTP reason. A failed tool request keeps the server's status and reason. Nod does not retry it. If the SSE stream closes, the next request opens a new connection. Ask Nod to connect a service it can't find in the app catalog. Nod proposes a way in, called an access path, and sends you a link to a private setup page. There, you paste a token or sign in. The model never sees the token. | Access path | What Nod calls | How it signs in | | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | MCP server | Tools on a public HTTPS MCP server, or a private one you enter | A token in a header, or OAuth sign-in | | HTTP API | A method and path on the API | A token in a header, or OAuth sign-in | | CLI | A command with arguments | Tokens and other settings in environment variables | Some services give each region or workspace its own MCP address, such as a separate EU address, each with its own sign-in. On those services, an account can only sign in through its own address. Nod picks the address from a workspace address you give it, or asks for your workspace address or region before it proposes a connection. If sign-in ends on the service's home page instead of returning to Nod, tell Nod your workspace address and start again, or select **Connect MCP** and enter the address for your region. Nod keeps the token encrypted in Vault, and the server adds it to each call. Results and errors remove plaintext, JSON-escaped and URL- or form-encoded representations of the token. A returned file containing any of those representations is withheld. Nod doesn't execute regular-expression constraints from an external MCP input schema. It removes `pattern` and `patternProperties` before local structural validation. When `patternProperties` is removed, local validation allows all dynamic property names. Nod also relaxes rules that depend on the removed patterns. These include exclusive alternatives, negation, conditional rules, and upper limits on matching array items. This includes rules that refer to shared definitions. Unrelated rules keep their checks. Literal values, defaults, and examples stay unchanged. The MCP server remains responsible for enforcing its complete input contract. ## How connected CLIs keep the token safe A CLI path declares where to install the tool from: - an npm package, - a PyPI package, installed with `pipx`, or - an HTTPS download of a release program or archive, with an optional `sha256` checksum. It also names the environment variables the tool reads its credentials from, such as `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. Each name must end in `TOKEN`, `KEY`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `_ID` or `_SID`, so it can't be a variable that loads code, such as `LD_PRELOAD`. A tool with several variables is its own connection. The setup page shows the source and one field per variable, so you can check it before you paste anything. A command runs for up to 59 minutes unless Nod asks for longer. Installing a missing CLI has its own 10-minute limit before that. When an install runs longer, the error says "The connected CLI install ran longer than its 600-second limit." ```mermaid flowchart LR source[Declared source
npm · PyPI · HTTPS] -- installs --> sealed[(Sealed install)] sealed --> runner[Runs as
its own user]:::go token[(Tokens in Vault)]:::accent -- its variables --> runner files[Workspace files]:::muted -. as arguments .-> runner runner -- text output --> Nod[Nod] ``` Nod installs each tool as its own Linux user, in a folder only that user can open, so neither the workspace user nor another connected tool can change it or read its token. Each run gets an environment built from scratch: a `PATH` with the sealed tool and system folders, a private temporary home and its credential variables. Nothing comes from the workspace user's files or settings. A program that the model writes or replaces in the workspace never receives the token. You can still pass workspace files as arguments, and the CLI returns text. ## Send and receive files To attach a workspace file to a Composio action, Nod passes `{workspaceFile, mimeType, name?}`. The server reads and checks the files and uploads them to Composio only when the action runs. If the trust check asks you first, nothing is uploaded until you say yes, and declining sends nothing. Each file can be up to 15 MB, and files in one action can total 90 MB. Your yes covers the exact files Nod showed you: if one is changed or deleted before the action runs, nothing is sent and Nod has to ask again. Files that apps send back, up to 90 MB each, are saved privately in the workspace one at a time. Nod sees each file's name, type and size, and up to four images of 5 MB or less. Nothing reaches your chat until Nod shares it. MCP servers, APIs and CLIs use their own upload methods. ## Every action goes through the trust check The [checker](/trust/approvals/) sees each call's arguments as Nod sends them: the method, path and body, the MCP tool and input, or the CLI arguments. For a saved API or MCP server it sees the path or tool, not the server's address. It runs reads and drafts, and anything else only when your words ask for it. Otherwise Nod asks you first. A call to an access path you haven't saved is refused before that, so Nod never asks you about it. ## Related resources - [Apps with Composio](/connect/apps/) - [Models](/connect/models/) - [Approvals and the trust check](/trust/approvals/) - [Vault and saved logins](/trust/vault/) - [Sandbox and browser](/how-it-works/sandbox-and-browser/)

---
title: Deploy and operate
description: Run one personal Nod server, connect your devices, and keep its configuration and data safe.
sidebar:
  order: 0
---

Run one Nod server for yourself, then use it from the web app, desktop app, Telegram, or WhatsApp.

Each server has one assistant and one owner. Everyone with its access token can use that assistant and its connected accounts.

## In this section

- [Host your own server](/deploy/self-host/): install the Docker stack and connect to it.
- [Choose a cloud server](/deploy/providers/): compare persistent VPS hosting and the limits of trial and disposable VM offers.
- [Deploy on boxd](/deploy/boxd/): use a community guide with its test scope, managed HTTPS setup, and operating limits.
- [Host on a Mac mini](/deploy/mac-mini/): run the same stack on your own Mac.
- [Back up and update a server](/deploy/server-operations/): preserve your data, restore it, and manage updates.
- [Configuration reference](/deploy/configuration/): environment variables, defaults, and precedence.
- [The desktop app](/deploy/desktop-app/): local runtime, data storage, and updates.
- [Analytics](/deploy/analytics/): what Nod collects and how to control it.
- [Troubleshooting](/deploy/troubleshooting/): diagnose setup and runtime problems.

---
title: Choose a cloud server
description: Choose a VPS for Nod, compare Hetzner and DigitalOcean, and understand Railway trial limits.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

Use a Linux virtual machine with Docker Engine and persistent disk storage. Hetzner and DigitalOcean can run the same Nod stack as a Mac mini. Railway has a separate VM sandbox product worth considering for short experiments.

Start with two CPU cores, 8 GB of memory, and 50 GB of disk. This is a starting size, not a measured minimum. Browser tasks and local models can need more capacity.

## Choose a provider

Offers checked on 2026-10-23. Verify eligibility, remaining credit, and the displayed price before creating resources. Model providers charge separately.

| Provider                                                                      | Use it for                                                              | Free offer and limits                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Hetzner Cloud](https://docs.hetzner.com/cloud/general/faq/)                  | A persistent VPS with control over Docker, storage, and firewall rules. | Paid hosting. Its referral-credit program has ended; don't rely on old free-credit links.                                                                  |
| [DigitalOcean](https://docs.digitalocean.com/platform/billing/signup-credit/) | A persistent VPS, or a short test covered by signup credit.             | The first team receives US$5 for 90 days. A valid payment method is required before creating a Droplet. Credit does not make continued hosting free.       |
| [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/pricing/free-trial)                        | A bounded VM experiment when capacity is available.                     | Anonymous VMs have 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, and a 60-minute build window. Registered trials receive US$5 for 30 days. VM lifecycle and memory limits still apply. |

If you need a free-only test, confirm the credit before starting and delete resources before it runs out. Hetzner is not a free-trial option under the terms above.

## Hetzner Cloud

1. Create a project and add your SSH public key. Choose Ubuntu 24.04 on an AMD64 or ARM64 server with at least 8 GB RAM and 50 GB of disk.
2. Check the price before creating it. [Hetzner bills allocated servers even when powered off](https://docs.hetzner.com/cloud/billing/faq/); removing a server and any separately allocated resources ends their charges.
3. Add a cloud firewall allowing SSH from your address. For public HTTPS, also allow inbound TCP 80 and 443.
4. Connect through SSH and [install Docker Engine with Compose](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/).
5. Follow [Host your own server](/deploy/self-host/). Open an SSH tunnel before local browser access, or configure a domain and HTTPS.

Use Nod's [backup procedure](/deploy/server-operations/#back-up) to preserve the database, files, and keys together. Keep a copy outside the VM.

## DigitalOcean

1. Check the [signup credit](https://docs.digitalocean.com/platform/billing/signup-credit/) in the Control Panel. Older guides advertising a standard US$200 credit do not describe the current offer.
2. [Create a Droplet](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/create/) with Ubuntu 24.04, at least two vCPUs, 8 GB RAM, and 50 GB persistent disk. Add your SSH public key. Check the hourly price and any optional paid resources before creation.
3. Add a cloud firewall allowing SSH from your address. For public HTTPS, also allow inbound TCP 80 and 443.
4. Connect through SSH, [install Docker Engine with Compose](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/), and follow [Host your own server](/deploy/self-host/).
5. For a disposable test, export a backup and remove the Droplet and related resources before the credit expires or runs out.

The normal Nod stack includes PostgreSQL. A managed database is optional and is not needed for this setup.

## Railway: understand the VM limits

Railway's [Sandboxes](https://docs.railway.com/sandboxes) are Linux VMs, separate from its ordinary deployed services. They [include a Docker daemon and CLI](https://railway.com/changelog/2026-06-12-docker-in-sandboxes), so running sibling containers is possible. Deploying Nod's server image as an ordinary Railway service alone does not create its Docker runtime, browser, or workspace.

Free and Trial Sandboxes are limited to two vCPUs and 2 GB RAM. They are destroyed after up to five idle minutes; only paid plans can disable that timeout. Active SSH, port-forwarding, or command sessions defer idle destruction. Background containers alone do not. Checkpoints preserve a disk snapshot, but they are not a replacement for a consistent database backup.

Railway also offers an [anonymous VM](https://railway.com/free-vm):

```sh title="Terminal"
ssh railway.new
```

It requires no account or card, identifies you by your SSH key, and gives you 60 minutes to build. There is then a 24-hour window to claim the VM; unclaimed files are deleted. The preview URL is restricted to your IP until claimed. Availability is capacity-dependent. This is a separate trial flow: its page does not guarantee a disk size or list Docker among its installed tools.

Before transferring Nod, check the VM:

```sh title="Remote terminal"
df -h
free -m
docker version
docker compose version
```

Use the [prebuilt bundle](/deploy/self-host/#install-a-prebuilt-bundle) matching the VM's Linux architecture. A 2 GB VM may run out of memory when building from source, and a successful installation does not establish that it has enough memory for your browser tasks. Keep the server configuration and token private.

Use a persistent VPS for an unattended assistant. Don't keep the only copy of your conversation, credentials, or files in a disposable trial VM. These Railway instructions describe the platform constraints; they do not establish a verified Nod deployment there.

## Other cloud accounts

The same installation works on a conventional Ubuntu VM from another provider. If you already have an eligible trial, these are alternatives:

| Provider                                                                                           | Suggested starting VM                                 | Trial terms                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [AWS Free plan](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/free-tier-plans.html) | Ubuntu 24.04, `m7i-flex.large`, 50 GB EBS.            | Eligible new customers receive US$100 plus up to US$100 through activities. Choose **Free plan**. It ends after six months or credit exhaustion. |
| [Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features)                        | Ubuntu 24.04, `e2-standard-2`, 50 GB persistent disk. | Eligible new customers receive US$300 for 90 days. Keep the trial plan; resources stop unless you upgrade.                                       |

Check [EC2 free-tier eligibility](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-free-tier-usage.html) or [Google's machine sizes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/general-purpose-machines#e2_machine_types) before choosing a VM. Small always-free machines have less memory than the starting size above. An existing paid account follows different billing rules.

## Community deployment guides

These guides describe setups tested by contributors. Check each guide's test scope and operating limits before you choose a provider.

- [Deploy on boxd](/deploy/boxd/): run Nod on a persistent VM with managed HTTPS. The guide includes the contributor's installation checks and the remaining operating checks.

## Finish the network setup

These steps apply to conventional VMs. For boxd, follow its [managed HTTPS instructions](/deploy/boxd/#install-nod) instead.

For public access, point a domain at the VM and use [Nod's HTTPS setup](/deploy/self-host/#add-public-https). Open only ports 80 and 443 for the proxy and keep SSH restricted. An SSH tunnel works without a domain.

Docker warns that published container ports can bypass `ufw` rules. Use the provider firewall too, and don't publish PostgreSQL, the browser, the workspace, or the Docker API. See [Docker's firewall limitations](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/#firewall-limitations).

Before a trial expires, export a backup and decide whether to move or keep the server. Stopping a VM can leave disks and addresses allocated. Follow the provider's removal flow when you finish a disposable test.

## Related resources

- [Deploy and operate](/deploy/)
- [Host your own server](/deploy/self-host/)
- [Back up and update a server](/deploy/server-operations/)
- [Host on a Mac mini](/deploy/mac-mini/)

---
title: Back up and update a server
description: Back up a self-hosted Nod server, restore into a fresh installation, update it, and rotate its access token.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

Keep your server configuration and data together, and make a backup before updating Nod.

Run the commands below from your bundle directory or `nod/deployment/self-host` source checkout. If you use the HTTPS profile, include `--profile https` in Compose start, stop, and status commands.

## Check and stop the server

```sh title="Terminal"
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail 100 server
```

To stop the stack without deleting data:

```sh title="Terminal"
docker compose stop
```

Start it again with `docker compose up -d --wait`. Don't use `docker compose down --volumes` or delete the installation's volumes unless you intend to remove its data.

## Back up

Wait for active work to finish. Keep your configuration in `.env`, remove shell overrides, and [apply configuration changes](/deploy/configuration/#how-settings-work) before making a backup. Backup and restore refuse `NOD_ENV_FILE` overrides in either the shell or saved configuration; they preserve the installation's `.env` only.

Choose a new backup directory whose parent already exists:

```sh title="Terminal"
sh backup.sh /absolute/path/to/nod-backup-2026-10-23
```

The command stops the server, browser, and workspace while it copies data. It resumes only the services that were running beforehand, including if the backup fails.

| Backup item              | What it preserves                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.env`                   | Server access token, Vault key, database password, and your environment settings.             |
| `postgres.dump`          | A logical PostgreSQL backup of conversations, settings, schedules, and encrypted credentials. |
| `server-data.tar.gz`     | Server state, transcripts, and local profile data.                                            |
| `workspace-data.tar.gz`  | Files created in Nod's workspace.                                                             |
| `workspace-tools.tar.gz` | Installed workspace tools and their files.                                                    |
| `browser-data.tar.gz`    | Browser profiles and saved browser state.                                                     |
| `source-commit`          | The bundle or source checkout revision to restore before starting Nod.                        |
| `complete`               | The marker required by the restore command.                                                   |

The destination must not exist. The command creates private files and refuses a custom `DATABASE_URL`. For an external database, coordinate its backup with copies of the four data volumes while Nod is stopped.

:::danger[The backup contains secrets]
Store it encrypted and restrict who can read it. Without the original Vault key, the database cannot recover saved credentials.
:::

Copy the backup off the server. TLS certificates are not included; Caddy obtains new certificates when a restored HTTPS installation starts.

## Restore into a fresh installation

Keep the original installation until you have checked the restore. The restore command refuses an existing `.env`, project containers, or project volumes.

1. Unpack your saved bundle into a new folder. Its `source-revision` must match the backup's `source-commit`. Don't run the installer yet.

   For a source installation, clone Nod into a new folder and check out that commit:

   ```sh title="Terminal"
   git clone https://github.com/n8n-io/nod.git nod-restored
   cd nod-restored
   git checkout <commit-from-source-commit>
   cd deployment/self-host
   ```

2. Restore under a new Compose project name. Don't run `setup.sh` first: the backup supplies the original keys.

   ```sh title="Terminal"
   sh restore.sh /absolute/path/to/nod-backup-2026-10-23 nod-restored
   ```

3. Review the restored `.env`. Set the new public address if it changed. If the original server still runs on this machine, select another `PORT`.
4. Stop the original server before starting the restored one. Two copies can run the same schedules or receive messages for the same bot.
5. Start the restored bundle:

   ```sh title="Bundle installation"
   sh install.sh
   ```

   Use `sh install.sh --https` for a public address. For a source checkout, rebuild and start:

   ```sh title="Terminal"
   docker compose up -d --build --wait
   ```

   For a public address, use `docker compose --profile https up -d --build --wait` instead.

The restore command restores file ownership and the original Vault key. It stops PostgreSQL afterwards and leaves the assistant stopped until you start it.

If configuration validation fails before data is restored, the command removes the newly created `.env` so you can correct the backup configuration and retry. A failure after restoration starts keeps the new project for inspection.

Open Nod with the saved token. Check conversation history, workspace files, model settings, and channel status. Check a saved credential through the private form without sending its value to chat. Review schedules before leaving the server running.

A restore returns data to the backup's point in time. It does not undo messages or actions that happened afterwards.

## Update a bundle

1. Download the new [private bundle](/deploy/self-host/#install-a-prebuilt-bundle) for the same architecture. Check the source commit in its release tag or workflow run, and verify the archive checksum.
2. Back up the server. Keep the old bundle with that backup.
3. Stop the whole stack with `docker compose --profile https stop`. This also includes Caddy when HTTPS is enabled.
4. From the parent of your installation directory, unpack the new bundle over the existing directory. The bundle doesn't contain `.env` or your data volumes.

   ```sh title="Parent of the installation directory"
   tar -xzf nod-server-linux-<architecture>-<new-commit>.tar.gz
   cd nod-server-linux-<architecture>
   sh install.sh
   ```

   For public HTTPS, use `sh install.sh --https`. The installer keeps your existing `.env`, checks the images, and starts them without compiling.

5. Open Nod, confirm its history and files, and check channel status.

The `source-revision` file records the installed bundle revision. Don't change `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` during an update: it selects your existing data volumes.

## Prepare a private server release

After maintainer approval, run the **Self-host bundle** workflow on `main` with **draft_release** selected. Package, container and deployment changes start bundle checks on pushes to `main`. The workflow also runs each week and on request. These runs leave the release option off and only create temporary workflow artifacts.

Both native architecture builds, server checks and standalone installer checks must pass before the release job runs. That job uses the existing `release` environment and its protection rules. It verifies each archive's checksum, source commit and architecture, creates `server-<full-source-commit>`, uploads both bundles and checks GitHub's asset digests. The result is an unpublished draft in the private repository.

Review the successful run, checksums and release notes before publishing the draft within the private repository. Drafts are only visible to maintainers; published releases are available to people with repository access. Neither step changes repository visibility. Release assets do not use the workflow's 14-day artifact retention.

The workflow never publishes or replaces an existing tag, release or asset. If a run stops after creating a tag or draft, inspect that partial result before retrying; a rerun refuses to overwrite it. Keep your own copy of each installed bundle with its backup even after a release is available.

## Update a source installation

1. Read the release notes and create a backup.
2. Stop the stack.
3. Check out the release tag or commit you want to run, then rebuild and start it.

   ```sh title="Terminal"
   docker compose stop
   git fetch origin --tags
   git checkout <release-tag-or-commit>
   docker compose up -d --build --wait
   ```

4. Open Nod, confirm its history and files, and check channel status.

The images build from the checked-out source. Pin a release or commit so you can identify what runs on the server. The setup command preserves your existing `.env`.

Database migrations run when Nod starts. Don't point an older application version at an already upgraded database. To roll back, restore the pre-update backup into a fresh installation using its recorded revision.

## Rotate access

Generate a replacement token on the server:

```sh title="Terminal"
openssl rand -hex 32
```

Replace `NOD_AUTH_TOKEN` in `.env`, then recreate the server:

```sh title="Terminal"
docker compose up -d --wait server
```

Reconnect web and desktop clients with the new token. The previous token no longer grants access. Channel credentials are separate.

Don't replace `NOD_VAULT_KEY` to rotate access. It encrypts saved credentials; changing it without re-encrypting those records makes them unreadable.

# Nod capability evals

Runs real tasks against the real Nod harness, with a real model, fake apps and lookalike websites, and reports how often Nod gets them right. Pi's `web_search` and `fetch_content` tools run on the server and still reach the public web. The evals call live models and cost money; unit tests never run them.

Read [Capability evals](../docs/src/content/docs/contribute/evals.mdx) for how scoring works, the CI workflow, the verdict rules, the scenario list and how to write and calibrate a scenario.

```sh
pnpm run eval:capability doctor --fix   # check Docker, images, database and keys
pnpm run eval:capability run --tier pr --repeat 1
pnpm run eval:capability help
```

# n8n workflows

This folder maintains five of Nod's workflows on the internal n8n instance. Each script here generates or embeds the exact workflow source, and each has synthetic contract tests.

| Workflow               | Source                           | What it does                                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nod Desktop Releases   | `desktop-releases.mjs`           | Serves published desktop releases, runtime packs and update feeds without exposing a GitHub token  |
| Nod Install            | `install-workflow.mjs`           | Serves `install.sh` for Mac Terminal and `install.ps1` for Windows PowerShell                      |
| Nod Feedback           | `feedback.mjs`                   | Turns in-app feedback into a Linear issue with its reports attached                                |
| Nod Traces             | `traces.mjs`                     | Forwards opted-in, scrubbed conversation traces to the `nod` LangSmith project in the EU           |
| Nod onboarding updates | `onboarding-updates.workflow.ts` | Records an unverified email signup and fixed About you choices in Customer.io Labs; sends no email |

```sh
node --test deployment/n8n/*.test.mjs
```

- The release broker only serves published `nod-v*` releases from this repository, pins each asset by release and asset ID, and never streams archives through n8n.
- The traces broker refuses requests without the `x-nod-traces-token` header from the n8n credential `nod traces webhook`, answers the rest with 202, validates each trace, forwards about 600 per clock minute in total (a best-effort cost cap: a burst across a minute boundary or simultaneous runs can pass a few more), pins each to that project by its ID as one `llm` run and keeps no execution data. Official desktop builds get the token from the `NOD_TRACES_TOKEN` release secret; anyone who unpacks the app can read it, so it keeps out scanners, not a determined sender. Its LangSmith service key lives only in the n8n credential `nod LangSmith traces`, never in Nod.
- The onboarding updates workflow exposes a public n8n webhook, accepts only versioned email submissions with a consent-checkbox claim and fixed About you choices, and rejects bodies over 2 KB after n8n parses them. Anyone can call the webhook, so the claim does not verify control of the address. The workflow stamps the receipt time on the server and identifies the person by normalized email in Customer.io Labs, where email is enabled as an identifier. Customer.io updates the existing profile or creates one if the address is new. Keep email identification enabled in Labs; otherwise the address can become a separate ID. The workflow uses the same Track API credential as Nod Waitlist, preserves unsubscribe state, and sends no message. Apply the retention settings in `onboarding-updates.settings.json` before publication. Do not send update emails until the double opt-in confirmation flow is ready.
- Feedback requests are versioned in `src/ports/feedback.ts`. The workflow checks every hash before it touches Linear, and repeated submissions with the same ID can't create a second issue. Execution data retention stays off.
- Older private builds use the release broker. Publish it before an installer that depends on it, and export the current workflow version before replacing it so you can roll back.
- Public builds and installers fetch GitHub Releases directly. Check that their installer, runtime pack, and update assets resolve before publishing a release. The n8n broker remains available for older private builds.

User-facing behaviour is documented in [Install the desktop app](../../docs/src/content/docs/get-started/install-desktop.mdx) and [Your data and privacy](../../docs/src/content/docs/trust/privacy.md).

title: Computer use
description: Let Nod use native apps on your computer, such as TextEdit, Numbers, Mail or Notepad, in work you start, with browsers view-only and risky apps always refused.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

Computer use lets Nod work in apps on your computer, for example to write a list in TextEdit, fill a table in Numbers or write a reply into a Mail draft. Nod reads each app's window through the system's accessibility service, the same information screen readers use, and presses its buttons, chooses its menu items and types into its fields. It works in the desktop app, using the open-source [agent-desktop](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop) tool bundled in the app, and never moves your pointer. It works in the background where it can, and brings an app to the front only for steps that need it; see [When Nod brings an app to the front](#when-nod-brings-an-app-to-the-front). A source install and a self-hosted server don't offer it.

Computer use is experimental on macOS, Windows and Linux: it hasn't been tested on many computers yet. Windows and Linux use the same checks as macOS; see [Windows and Linux](#windows-and-linux) for what differs.

Nod uses computer use last. When a [connected app](/connect/apps/) can do the work, Nod uses it, even when you name the service: "message Priya on Slack" goes through your Slack connection. It uses the app on your computer instead only when you ask for it, such as "in the Slack app on my Mac", or when no connection can do the work, for example when Slack isn't connected but its app is on your computer. For files Nod uses [local files](/connect/local-files/), and for other websites its own browser.

## Turn it on

1. Open **Settings**, **Computer use**, and turn on **Let Nod use apps on this Mac** (**on this computer** on Windows and Linux).
2. On macOS, select **Allow** next to **Accessibility**. macOS opens **System Settings**, **Privacy & Security**, **Accessibility**. Turn on Nod there.
3. On macOS, optionally select **Allow** next to **Screen Recording** the same way. Nod then can take a picture of one app window when its controls don't show what it needs, for example formatting.

Windows needs no permission. On Linux, the desktop's accessibility service must be running; Settings tells you when Nod can't reach it.

Turning computer use off stops it at once and forgets every app Nod opened.

## Start with a request

Tell Nod which app to use and what to do:

- "Open TextEdit and write a shopping list: milk, bread, eggs."
- "Make a table of these numbers in Numbers."
- "In the reply to Lena that's open in Mail, write that I'll be there on Friday. Don't send it."

Nod opens an app only when your words name it or ask for work that needs it. Opening one counts like opening a file: when your words don't cover it, Nod asks first. The app stays open to Nod for the rest of that request, and a task started from it, but not for later requests. To let Nod use an app whenever it needs it, add a [rule](/trust/approvals/), such as "Nod may use Numbers without asking".

## What Nod can do

| Action           | What it does                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| List apps        | Lists running apps. It shows window titles only for apps Nod opened in this request.                               |
| Open             | Launches an app in the background, or picks one that is already running.                                           |
| Read a window    | Reads the window's controls, labels and text, or the app's menu bar. A busy window comes back as an outline first. |
| Picture a window | Takes a picture of that one window, never the whole screen. It needs Screen Recording.                             |
| Press, choose    | Presses a button or chooses a menu item.                                                                           |
| Type             | Sets or types the text of a field, or picks an option.                                                             |
| Key              | Sends a shortcut, such as Cmd+N, to that app only.                                                                 |

Each step that can change content goes through the same [trust check](/trust/approvals/) as a connected app action. The check receives the app, window, control, proposed input, and current accessible window content. This includes existing recipients and message text, not only what Nod typed. Text entry is checked too: it can replace a selection or save at once. Only reading and moving focus run without this check.

Before input, Nod reads the window again. It refuses the step if the window content or control changed after the check. It checks again after waiting to bring an app forward. Keyboard input also stays bound to the focused control. In a list, table, outline, grid, tree or menu of more than 20 items, such as an inbox or a month view, the check sees only the item Nod acts on and the selected item, so new messages arriving elsewhere don't stop the step. When list items are left out, a send or submission runs without asking only when the checked window itself shows its recipients and message and your words cover them. A step can't run when the accessibility service returns an incomplete window, when the control is no longer in the window, or when the checked content exceeds 24,000 characters.

A step that waits for your answer, that you declined, or whose outcome is uncertain still blocks the same control in that app for the rest of the request, even after the window changes. Stopping work cancels its queued steps, and no step starts after its deadline, so a step reported as not run can't run later.

## What Nod never does

Nod refuses these, without a judgment call. It recognizes apps by their ID and program, so an app that isn't on its list isn't refused automatically; [keep Nod out of it](#keep-nod-out-of-an-app) instead:

- Terminals and apps that run scripts or commands, such as Terminal, iTerm, Script Editor, Automator, Shortcuts, Raycast, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, PowerShell and GNOME Terminal.
- System settings and security, such as System Settings, Keychain Access, Activity Monitor, Disk Utility and macOS security prompts, Windows Settings, Control Panel, Registry Editor and Task Manager, and GNOME or KDE Settings, Passwords and Keys, and Disks.
- File managers: Finder, File Explorer, Files (Nautilus) and Dolphin. Nod works with your files only through [local files](/connect/local-files/), with its protections. An app Nod may use can still open and save files through its own Open and Save panels, which local files would refuse; [keep Nod out of that app](#keep-nod-out-of-an-app) if that matters.
- Password managers, such as Passwords and 1Password, and crypto wallets.
- Nod itself.
- An app whose name another running app shares, or on Windows and Linux one with neither an app ID nor a program, because Nod can't tell which app it is.
- On macOS, the Apple menu, with Restart, Shut Down, Log Out and System Settings, and each app's own menu, with Services. Nod never shows them to the model.
- System shortcuts, such as Spotlight, Force Quit, Log Out and Lock Screen, any shortcut with the Windows or Super key, Alt+Tab, Ctrl+Alt+Delete and Ctrl+Alt+T.
- Any app you keep Nod out of.

Web browsers, such as Chrome and Safari, and code editors, such as VS Code, are view-only: Nod can read them but never presses, types or chooses anything there. For websites Nod uses [its own browser](/use/browser/), with your Vault and its safety checks.

Nod never reads or types into password fields: it checks the field again right before input, and sends no shortcut and takes no picture of an app while a password field has focus. To sign in somewhere, Nod uses [Vault](/trust/vault/) in its own browser.

## See when Nod uses an app

Nod works in the background where it can, so you can keep working. While it reads or acts in an app behind your windows, a small pill at the top of your screen says **Nod is working in** and the app's name. It stays until a few seconds after Nod's last step there. Select **Stop** on the pill, or press Cmd+Shift+Esc anywhere (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Esc on Windows and Linux), to stop all of Nod's work at once.

## When Nod brings an app to the front

Some steps only work with the app in front: keyboard shortcuts, typing into a message body such as in Mail, and on macOS anything in apps built on Chromium or Electron, such as Slack, Notion or Teams, which don't update while they're behind other windows. On Windows, typing always needs the app in front.

For those steps, Nod waits until you stop typing or moving the pointer for a moment, then brings only that window to the front. While it works there:

- A pink glow frames the window, and a pill below it says **Nod is using** and the app's name.
- Select **Stop** on the pill, or press Cmd+Shift+Esc anywhere (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Esc on Windows and Linux), to stop all of Nod's work at once.
- Keep your hands off the keyboard: what you type goes to the app in front. If you keep typing, Nod doesn't take over and the step doesn't run.

Afterwards Nod gives focus back to the window you were using, unless you've already switched to another one. To type into a message body, or into an app such as Slack, Nod pastes the text and then puts back what was on your clipboard. Clipboard history apps can still record the pasted text.

## Windows and Linux

The checks and refusals on Windows and Linux are the same as on macOS. What differs:

- **App IDs.** Nod names apps by their program name on Windows, such as `notepad.exe`, and by their desktop ID on Linux, such as `org.gnome.TextEditor`. On Linux it opens only installed desktop apps, never a command, a terminal, or a system, settings or file manager app; an app that's already open is checked only against Nod's list. On Windows it starts only windowed programs, never a command-line tool.
- **Windows:** Nod can read but not operate an app that runs as administrator.
- **Linux on Wayland:** Nod can't bring a window to the front, so steps that need it don't run, and it shows only the pill, without the glow. The Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Esc shortcut may not work there; select **Stop** on the pill instead.
- **Linux Flatpak:** computer use doesn't work in the Flatpak app yet. agent-desktop identifies the desktop's accessibility service through the host's process list, which the Flatpak sandbox hides, so it can't reach other apps ([agent-desktop issue #593](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/issues/593)). Settings shows this when you turn computer use on.

## Keep Nod out of an app

Tell Nod, for example "never use Messages", in a chat or a task you started. Nod adds the app to a list of up to 100 apps it always refuses. Only you can take an app off the list again, in **Settings**, **Computer use**. Nod can't remove one.

## Only work you started

Nod uses apps only in work you started: a message you sent, a task that started from one, or a schedule you set up. Work Nod starts on its own, such as on new email, can't use apps at all, and neither can helpers Nod starts inside a task. So a message from a stranger can't make Nod use your apps.

## Limits

- Text in app windows reaches Nod as data, not instructions. A window can still contain text written to mislead Nod, like any web page or email. The trust check limits what such text can make Nod do, but it can't recognize every trick, so keep apps with untrusted content out of Nod's reach when you don't need them.
- The list of refused apps is by app. An app that isn't on it but can run commands or reach your secrets, such as a database tool, is not recognized; keep such apps out of Nod.
- Window text and pictures go to your model provider like any other tool result, and are part of [conversation traces](/trust/conversation-traces/) when you share them. Pictures are replaced with `[image]` there. Window pictures aren't redacted: whatever is visible in the window, private content included, reaches the model. Only Vault entry in Nod's own browser keeps secrets out.
- The check can see only what the accessibility service provides. Apps can hide content from that service. A window can also change between the last check and the operating system receiving input.
- Apps that draw their own controls, such as some games, show little to accessibility. Nod can't use them.
